title: Purge-to-Spool Toll Recycler for Print Farms
one_liner: A mail-in service that turns multicolour purge waste and failed prints into laser-checked, guaranteed-diameter filament, so print farms get spools back without owning or babysitting a $1,200-$1,700 recycling rig.
customer: Print farms and Etsy print sellers running Bambu-style multicolour printers, maker spaces, schools and STEM programmes that produce kilograms of purge and failed prints monthly. Payer is the print-farm owner.
problem: Multicolour printing generates heavy purge waste, and existing recycling only pays in store credit. The DIY route (Creality's shredder plus filament maker) has diameter, jam and ROI risks that backers already worry about.
solution: Prepaid bins ship to the customer, who tosses in purge, supports and failed prints (same-polymer sorting only: PLA, PETG). The central facility shreds, dries, extrudes and spools with an inline laser micrometer, and returns a share of the weight as certified filament (for example a 1.75mm +/-0.03mm 'galaxy' random-colour spool). The remainder is sold as premium recycled filament. Customers see kg diverted and a certificate for 'green' Etsy claims.
why_now: Multicolour printing exploded (each Bambu Cube-style multicolour test can burn about 70 g of purge), and Creality's Filament Maker M1 and Shredder R1 hit its Indiegogo goal in 16 minutes and raised $6.8M from 5,320 backers, so waste is a felt problem. The first real-world tests show the DIY loop is not yet dependable, leaving a gap for a professional processor.
revenue_model: $3/kg intake fee (or pay-per-bin at $115 as Printerior's prepaid bins do), plus margin on selling recycled spools at $12-18/kg, plus a B2B subscription of $79-$199/mo for farms wanting monthly pickup and returns.
non_obvious_insight: Hobbyists backed a $649-$1,699 recycler, but the machine's own pre-production data shows why a service beats owning one. One reviewer measured filament diameter varying 1.78 mm to 1.58 mm across a single spool, and a complex print jammed at 97% recycled content. Creality itself recommends a 1:1 blend, and backers question ROI after electricity, failures and maintenance (https://makers101.com/creality-filament-maker-m1-shredder-r1-live-tracker/, raise figure of $6,816,733 from 5,320 backers; note that https://www.tcf.team/blog/q1-2026-crowdfunding-report reports a different $36M figure, so the exact total is uncertain, but demand is clear either way). Existing recyclers pay only points (Printerior: 280 points/kg redeemable for filament, and it requires sorted PLA/PLA+/PETG, https://printeriordesigns.com/pages/recycling), yet Printerior sells $114.99 prepaid bins, so people already pay to dispose responsibly. Nobody offers cash or spec-guaranteed spools back.
first_30_days: Buy a used 1.75mm extruder line, a shredder and a laser micrometer (about $6-10K) or rent time at a plastics co-op. Recruit 5 local print farms and 2 school maker labs as free pilots. Run 200 kg through, test diameter and print reliability in a 1:1 virgin blend, and photograph results. Then open pre-orders for prepaid bins ($115) and monthly pickup on the Bambu and Etsy-seller subreddits.

title: Teleoperated Pack-and-Pick Robots Piloted from Latin America
one_liner: Robot arms run by foundation models, with remote pilots in Guatemala or Colombia fixing the edge cases, sold per box.
customer: Berry, tomato and cucumber packhouses and greenhouses that lost crews.
problem: Farm labor shrank by at least 155,000 and crews were lost in 2026 harvests, while robots pick at 50-60% of human speed and fail on edge cases.
solution: Rent arms with a vision-language-action stack for clamshell packing, and route failures to remote operators at roughly one pilot per 8-10 arms, priced per case.
why_now: Physical-AI models matured in 2025-26, remote-assist tooling and satellite or 5G links are cheap, and enforcement removed the informal labor pool.
revenue_model: Per-case fee with a minimum monthly commitment per station.
non_obvious_insight: Robots run about 20 hours a day at half human speed, and remote humans fix the rare failures. The result is a labor channel that needs neither a visa nor a robot that never fails.
first_30_days: Rent two arms, set up a clamshell-packing station at one packhouse, and hire three remote operators for a paid pilot.

title: Resident Proof for Two-Tier Tourist Pricing
one_liner: A privacy-preserving QR proof of residence lets towns, museums and transit charge visitors more and locals less without building databases or discriminating by nationality.
customer: Municipalities and municipal attractions, ferries and parking in overrun towns of 5-100K people (Italy, Croatia, Spain, Japan), then private attractions and restaurants offering locals-first pricing.
problem: Insiders think dual pricing is a legal and PR minefield, useful only in niche places. It is spreading (reported moves include Rome's charge for non-resident visitors at the Trevi Fountain and resident-versus-visitor pricing at some Japanese castles). The real bottleneck is verification. Each site checks IDs by hand, builds a one-off app or discriminates crudely.
solution: Issue a wallet pass from the municipal residents' register, first over the town hall counter and later through national digital-ID wallets. It discloses only 'resident of X'. Gates and apps verify it offline, and the same pass unlocks locals-first booking windows and discounts. The town gets analytics on non-resident flows to tune fees.
why_now: Venice's flat fee reportedly did not reduce numbers, so cities are turning to differentiated pricing. EU member states must offer digital identity wallets by the end of 2026, which makes selective-disclosure credentials mainstream. Resident backlash is at its peak.
revenue_model: Municipal SaaS of EUR 10-30K per year, EUR 0.01-0.05 per verification, and an integration fee per attraction.
non_obvious_insight: Pricing policy is not the bottleneck; identity is. Whoever standardises the 'resident' claim owns the tollbooth for every future visitor-management rule, including resident-first windows, non-resident caps and local discounts.
first_30_days: Approach one town of 5-20K people that runs a municipal attraction, ferry or car park. Offer a free 90-day pilot where staff issue passes at the town hall and verify them with phone cameras. Use mayors' associations to find the pilot, and have a lawyer confirm the residency-based structure is proportionate.

title: Protein Cartridges for Heavy Rare-Earth Polishing
one_liner: Skid-mounted cartridges of engineered lanmodulin-type proteins that separate heavy rare earths (Dy, Tb) from magnet-recycling leachate without long solvent-extraction chains.
customer: Magnet recyclers and small separators whose processes end in mixed rare-earth concentrates, plus DoD- and DOE-backed pilot programs.
problem: Recovery projects often end with mixed concentrates that still need separation, which conventionally takes hundreds of solvent-extraction stages that China dominates. Heavy rare earths are the acute chokepoint after China's 2025 export controls.
solution: Protein-based sorbents (naturally lanthanide-binding proteins, studied at Penn State and Lawrence Livermore) engineered for heavy-RE selectivity. They are packed in modular columns as a polishing step at ambient conditions. The business model is cartridge consumables plus skid rental.
why_now: Heavy rare earths are now a stated national-security bottleneck, DOE announced $134M for demonstrations in June 2026, and AI protein design has made engineering selectivity a computation problem instead of a decade-long screen.
revenue_model: Consumable cartridge sales plus skid lease. Early revenue from SBIR grants and paid pilots.
non_obvious_insight: Rare-earth chemistry fights in a sea of near-identical ions, while proteins evolved to tell lanthanides apart. The hard part is now designing the scaffold, not discovering the effect.
first_30_days: License or partner with a university lab. Run bench tests on real recycler leachate. Apply to DOE and DoD SBIR programs. Sign 2 recyclers to paid pilots.

title: Licensing Workbench for Smallsat Operators
one_liner: A structured software system of record for satellite licensing across spectrum, debris, remote sensing and export control.
customer: Smallsat startups, university missions and new sovereign programs that currently pay law firms and consultants $50-300k per licensing cycle.
problem: Launches and deployments are at record levels (4,517 satellites in 2025), and licensing throughput is the hidden bottleneck. Operators juggle FCC, ITU, NOAA remote-sensing, debris-mitigation and export-control filings. Rules are changing (reported FCC rewrite, the 5-year deorbit rule, the proposed EU Space Act).
solution: A workbench with deterministic calculators (debris assessment, collision probability), templated filings, an ITU coordination tracker, deadline management and an insurer-ready data pack. Add a marketplace to hire specialist counsel. It is not a thin AI wrapper: the value is the structured filing data model and up-to-date rules.
why_now: The 2025-26 regulatory changes and a growing flood of new operators. The EU Space Act, FCC modernization and stricter debris rules all raise the compliance load.
revenue_model: $1-3k per month per mission. Per-filing fees. Referral fees from counsel and consultants.
non_obvious_insight: Every launch boom makes regulatory throughput the binding constraint. The company that owns the data model of a filing becomes the system of record.
first_30_days: Interview 15 smallsat licensing leads about their last filing. Build one calculator plus a deadline tracker for a specific filing, for example an FCC debris assessment. Sign five paying pilots at $500-1,000 per month.

title: Human-Review Receipts for the EU Text Exemption
one_liner: Sell signed proof that a named human reviewed and took responsibility for AI-assisted text, which is the thing the EU's disclosure rule for text appears to reward, not labels on AI.
customer: Newsletter operators, niche and local publishers, and B2B content agencies that publish AI-assisted text to EU readers. Second buyers are legal and compliance leads at mid-market publishers.
problem: The industry reads EU AI Act Art. 50 (applicable Aug 2, 2026) as 'label the AI.' My understanding of Art. 50(4) is that the text-disclosure duty for public-interest publications has an exemption where content underwent human review or editorial control and a person holds editorial responsibility. Confirm the exact wording with counsel, because the brief does not quote it. Meanwhile readers get accusation tools: Substack embedded Pangram scanning on Jul 22 and LinkedIn added a slop-report button on Jul 30. Publishers have no defensible record of human review.
solution: A Ghost, WordPress and Substack-compatible plugin plus API that records, per article, the AI draft versus the final diff, who reviewed it, and a passkey-signed approval bound to the content hash. It publishes a verification page and a byline element ('reviewed and edited by [name]'), and generates an evidence binder for regulators and clients. If no review is recorded, it falls back to an automatic disclosure line.
why_now: Art. 50 became applicable on Aug 2, 2026, and reader-side detection has just been built into major platforms. The first regulatory questions and client audits will land on publishers this year.
revenue_model: $29-99/month per publication, $500-2,000/month agency plans, and $250 per audit-ready evidence binder.
non_obvious_insight: Detection tries to prove a negative ('not AI'). The law's structure turns human review into a legal safe harbor, so the sellable product is a positive: a named person accepted responsibility. That gives 'human-made' a compliance budget instead of an ethics budget.
first_30_days: Ship a Ghost/WordPress plugin with diff capture and passkey sign-off in about three weeks. Approach 10 EU-facing newsletters and 3 agencies with 'Aug 2 has passed, where is your evidence?' Co-brand the evidence binder with one EU tech-law boutique that can use it as a channel.

title: The 40 Days: Postpartum Confinement Caregiver Guild
one_liner: A trained, insured, tradition-certified caregiver guild delivering the 26 to 42 day postpartum confinement (yuesao, sanhujori, cuarentena) to diaspora families whose grandmothers are far away.
customer: New parents in Chinese, Korean, Vietnamese, South Asian, Latino and Middle Eastern communities in dense metros, mostly mothers at 30 to 36 weeks. Secondary payers: extended-family gift funds and employers or health plans looking to reduce postpartum depression.
problem: Confinement care is widely practiced but supplied through informal agencies and word of mouth. A US yuesao runs about $200 to $400 a day for the standard 26 days, and a 42-day term adds roughly 60%. Quality, safety and worker protections vary widely, agencies rarely serve non-Chinese traditions, and parents without a grandmother nearby are left choosing between exhaustion and a gray-market caregiver.
solution: Build the guild rather than a marketplace. Recruit experienced caregivers and give them W-2 employment, insurance and background checks, plus training in safe sleep, lactation basics, infection control and postpartum warning signs with an escalation path to the family's OB or midwife. Certify them in specific traditions (menus, do's and don'ts) and match on language and tradition. Sell modular tiers: nights only, meals only, 14, 28 or 42 days. Add a plain-language guide for in-laws and partners.
why_now: Immigrant-heavy metros have a large unmet pool of families who want the ritual, and grandmothers are harder to bring over given tighter visa and travel rules. Employer-of-record and payroll tools make W-2 caregiver employment easy for a tiny company. Postpartum mental health is a rising priority for employers and health plans.
revenue_model: $5,500 to $12,000 per family per engagement, at about 30% to 35% gross margin after caregiver pay. Meals-only tier at $35 to $55 a day for faster revenue. Employer or plan subsidy of $1,000 to $2,000 per birth. A gift registry for extended family.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input is the trusted caregiver, so the moat is a certified workforce (training, payroll, insurance, safety escalation), not a listing site. Confinement is also the same intervention American medicine now calls the fourth trimester, so obstetric practices can refer to it without endorsing folk claims, and it has been an informal cash market that has never been professionalized.
first_30_days: Pick one metro with a dense Chinese-American or Korean-American community such as the San Gabriel Valley, Flushing or the Bay Area. Recruit 8 experienced caregivers through WeChat groups and existing agencies. Write a three-day training and safety protocol with a postpartum nurse and lactation consultant. Sign 10 founding families with a service guarantee, and sell a meals-only tier to 50 families for faster revenue. Line up two OB practices or doulas for referrals, and set up employer-of-record payroll.

title: Drone-Checked Eruv Boundaries
one_liner: Scheduled autonomous drone inspection of the utility-wire boundaries that define an eruv, so communities learn before Shabbat whether a line is down.
customer: Eruv committees and synagogues in the US and abroad (hundreds of communities), plus Jewish federations and city-level committees.
problem: An eruv's boundary is often miles of utility wire, checked weekly by volunteers on foot or by car. A break invalidates carrying on Shabbat, and storms and tree limbs cause breaks. Utilities do not notify committees.
solution: Weekly autonomous flights (drone-in-a-box under Part 107 first, then BVLOS), computer-vision detection of wire discontinuity and pole damage, and GPS-pinned photo alerts to the committee. The rabbinic authority stays the decision-maker, and the tool provides the time-stamped evidence.
why_now: The FAA's Part 108 BVLOS rule cleared to OIRA (final review) in July 2026 and was not yet published as of mid-September. Drone docks and vision models are cheap. A 2016 proposal in Israel showed interest but no commercial product surfaced.
revenue_model: $300-1,500/month per eruv plus a setup fee, then adjacent inspection contracts (cemetery and campus perimeters, congregation roofs and steeples).
non_obvious_insight: The religious need is verification, not construction. A weekly audit trail with time-stamped imagery is exactly what a committee needs for its Friday declaration, which converts a religious-legal requirement into a recurring inspection budget line.
first_30_days: Contact 5 eruv committees (for example Baltimore, Teaneck, Cleveland). Fly VLOS segments with a Part 107 pilot, build a wire-break detection dataset, and sign 2 paid pilots at about $250/month.

title: Router-and-Breaker Screen Control Sold by Trades
angle: Pairing 2: Construction/housing/skilled-trades/home services x Parenting/childcare deserts/Gen Alpha/kids and AI-screens
one_liner: HVAC, electrical and plumbing shops install tamper-proof, infrastructure-level screen and AI-companion controls as a maintenance-plan add-on for families with kids 8-15.
customer: Home-service shops with 5-30 techs and a maintenance-plan base (they resell the kit), and the parents of 8-15-year-olds who pay $199-349 to install plus $12-18 a month. Slow-season HVAC shops are the first wave.
problem: Under-16 social bans and school phone rules leak: VPNs cost under A$20 a month, seven in ten Australian under-16s reportedly still hold accounts, and only 29% of parents planned full compliance. App-level controls live on the device the kid controls, so they get uninstalled, and they cannot touch consoles, smart TVs, AI toys or AI companion sites. Parents want enforcement kids cannot delete. Meanwhile HVAC shipments fell 25-50% and shops have idle techs and a need for recurring revenue.
solution: A standard 'family network' kit installed in one visit, built from a hardwired or mesh router with router-level policies (VPN and proxy blocking, AI-companion and social categories by age tier, per-device schedules, guest SSID), plus smart-relay outlets ('kid circuits') for consoles and TVs, and a phone-parking charging nook. Parents manage it in a simple app, and shops get a two-hour training course and a quarterly tune-up visit. Cellular data is honestly disclosed as out of scope, and the kit aims at evenings and nights at home.
why_now: Bans and age-assurance rules are live in Australia, Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Texas and Ohio, and Australia is proposing to double fines, so enforcement is the gap. The FTC's 2025 6(b) inquiry and state AI-companion laws put AI chatbots at the center of parental worry. HVAC is at a trough until a 2027 rebound, so shops want add-on services now.
revenue_model: Hardware-plus-install margin split with shops (about $75 spiff plus 30-40% of install), $12-18 per household per month recurring, and training and certification fees for shops.
non_obvious_insight: Software controls sit on the device kids control, so enforcement has to move to infrastructure parents physically own, and installing infrastructure is a trades skill. A local HVAC shop with 2,000 plan customers, most of them families, has near-zero customer acquisition cost compared with consumer parental-control apps.
first_30_days: Build the kit on off-the-shelf router hardware with DNS and VPN filtering and smart relays. Train two local electrical or HVAC shops and pilot 20 installs with a $75 spiff. Log bypass attempts and parent satisfaction, then sign five more shops using the pilot's numbers.

title: Drone Incident Desk for Cities and Venues
one_liner: Detection-to-handoff service that turns a drone sighting into a documented, legally routed federal referral for local agencies that cannot legally jam anything.
customer: City emergency management and police departments, stadium and arena operators, and event promoters at major events. Dallas has $10M set aside, and FEMA has a $500M counter-UAS grant program.
problem: Insiders see counter-drone as a radar and jammer hardware sale. Local police mostly lack legal authority to mitigate, and protocols with FBI and DHS are unclear. FBI and DHS seized more than 700 drones near one stadium during the World Cup. Cities are buying sensors with no playbook for what to do next.
solution: Vendor-neutral software plus a 24/7 human desk. It ingests alerts from whatever sensors a venue owns (RF, Remote ID, radar) and classifies them. It geolocates the pilot, routes the incident to the correct federal or state authority, and packages a chain-of-custody evidence file. Includes tabletop drills and after-action reports.
why_now: The World Cup exposed the gap. FEMA counter-UAS grant money is arriving at localities. Future mega-events raise urgency, and Remote ID data is now broadly available.
revenue_model: Annual subscription per venue or city ($40-150K), event-surge packages, and drill or training fees. It also helps grant applicants justify sensor purchases.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is purchasing liability cover and a working relationship with federal agencies, not detection accuracy. Sensors will commoditize, but the handoff protocol and evidence trail will not.
first_30_days: Interview 10 emergency managers and venue security directors in World Cup host cities. Build the desk on a shared inbox plus a case-management tool. Offer a free tabletop exercise to 3 venues and convert one to a paid pilot.

title: First-72-Hours Concierge for Paid Communities
one_liner: An outcome-priced service that staffs experienced ex-power-mods to personally handle every new member's first three days in creator-run paid communities, cutting the week-one churn that drains recurring revenue.
customer: Owners of paid communities with 500-20,000 paying members on Skool, Circle, Discord, Mighty Networks or Patreon: course creators and trading, fitness and business coaches doing $50k-$1M+ per month.
problem: Skool operator guides say about 60% of churners decide in week one, and average monthly churn sits around 12-18%. Owners cover the front door with random volunteers or VAs posting templated welcomes. New members' first posts go unanswered for a day. Scam DMs from fake admins ('send USDT to verify') hit newcomers hardest. The first unexplained removal or cold reply turns a paying member into a refund request.
solution: Small pods of trained ex-moderators run the first 72 hours: a personal welcome, a reply to every first post within 2 hours across time zones, routing to the right thread, removal of impersonators and scam DMs, and gentle handling of first-time rule breaks so the person stays. AI drafts and triages, but a human always sends. Each community gets a rules-as-code playbook and a weekly cohort-retention report with a holdout group so the effect is measurable. Work stays on Discord, Skool and Circle, so it doesn't collide with Reddit's Rule 5.
why_now: Reddit began enforcing its five-community moderator cap on 31 March 2026. That has pushed many experienced volunteer mods into Advisor/Alumni roles and left them open to paid work on platforms the cap doesn't cover. Creator-run paid communities have grown into real revenue businesses, while AI slop and scam DMs make the new-member experience worse.
revenue_model: A base fee of $1.5k-$4k per month per community plus an outcome kicker of 10-20% of retained MRR uplift versus a holdout. Mods are paid $15-$25 per hour, giving roughly 40-50% gross margin.
non_obvious_insight: In big subreddits a newcomer whose first comment is removed without explanation almost never returns. Retention is decided in the first three days by one human interaction, not by content quality. That makes moderation a retention function, not a cost center, so it should be priced by churn saved, not hours worked. It is also hard to outsource to a generic trust-and-safety BPO, because tone and judgment are the product.
first_30_days: Recruit 10-15 ex-power-mods from mod Discords and r/ModSupport who lost seats under the cap. Write a one-page playbook. Approach 30 owners of Skool communities with 1k+ paying members, using the public discovery listings. Offer a $750, 14-day pilot in which half of new joiners get the concierge and half don't. Report the day-14 retention delta and convert the best results into monthly contracts.

title: Insurability Index and Tax-Base Hedge for Towns
one_liner: Measure insurance withdrawal town by town, then hedge municipal property-tax bases against it.
customer: Municipal finance officers of small towns, school districts and special districts in Florida, California and Colorado. Muni bond funds, community banks and rating analysts buy the data.
problem: When insurance leaves, home values fall, the tax base erodes and bonds reprice, yet nobody measures insurability itself. FAIR and Citizens policy counts, nonrenewal filings and rate filings are public but fragmented. Physical-risk scoring is commoditizing (MSCI-First Street), but insurance availability is not measured.
solution: A monthly ZIP and county Insurability Index (FAIR or Citizens share, nonrenewal filings, carrier appetite, premium-to-value), sold to muni investors, community banks and appraisers. In year two, add index-linked parametric tax-base protection backed by ILS capital, paying towns when the index crosses agreed thresholds.
why_now: Cat bonds are at record scale (about $65.6B outstanding with 12 first-time sponsors), FAIR keeps growing, and physical-risk data is consolidating while insurance availability is unmeasured.
revenue_model: $10-50K data subscriptions, then structuring fees and hedge premium.
non_obvious_insight: The financial risk is insurance withdrawal, not physical damage. It is measurable from public regulator data, and municipal budgets are unhedged against it.
first_30_days: Build the index for California and Florida counties from public data. Send it monthly to 20 muni analysts and community bankers, and convert the first subscribers.

title: Notarized Sky: Satellite Image Authenticity Desk
angle: Pairing 2: Space economy x Cybersecurity/identity fraud (deepfakes)
one_liner: A verification desk that tells insurers, traders and newsrooms whether a 'satellite photo' is real, by corroborating it against independent archives and issuing a signed chain-of-custody attestation.
customer: Marine war-risk and political-violence underwriters and brokers in the London market, commodity and energy trading desks, and verification desks at wire services and OSINT outlets. Second wave: parametric insurers whose triggers depend on Earth-observation data, and arbitration or sanctions law firms.
problem: Generative tools can now fabricate or subtly edit overhead imagery, and viral 'satellite photos' of strikes, burning tankers or troop moves circulate in every conflict, moving prices and claims. Buyers assume satellites are physics-grade truth, but the last mile is a JPEG on social media and vendors sell pixels, not provenance. With the Strait of Hormuz reportedly closed since March 2026, war-risk claims and rumor-driven price moves are large.
solution: (1) Rapid 'witness triangulation': check the claimed place and time against open archives (Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2, Landsat) and quick commercial archive pulls (optical and SAR), plus sun-angle and shadow geometry, cloud and terrain consistency, and vessel positions versus AIS and RF logs. (2) Forensics for synthetic or edited artifacts and C2PA/EXIF provenance. (3) A signed, hash-timestamped corroboration report usable in claims files and disputes. (4) For imagery buyers, verify delivered files against provider manifests.
why_now: Hormuz disruption created a wave of unverifiable incident claims. EU AI Act Article 50(2) synthetic-content marking applies from 2 Dec 2026 for systems already on the market, raising attention on provenance. Commodity EO and SAR are cheap and frequent (Planet targets up to 10 revisits a day), but no cross-vendor 'signed pixels' standard exists.
revenue_model: $2.5-8K per rapid verification report (24-hour SLA) and $8-20K per month retainers for underwriters and desks. Later, metered API access for parametric insurers.
non_obvious_insight: Detection accuracy is not the product; corroboration is. Government-held archives cannot be retroactively edited by an attacker, and SAR sees through cloud and is not something a text-to-image model can fake convincingly. A tiny team can be an independent witness cheaply. What buyers actually pay for is a defensible attestation, a SOC report for pixels, that survives a claims dispute.
first_30_days: Publish teardowns of 3 viral fake or misattributed satellite images from 2025-26 conflicts, each with reproducible multi-source refutations. Send them to 25 marine war-risk brokers and 15 newsroom verification desks. Sell 3 rapid-verification pilots at $2.5K each and convert one underwriter to a retainer.

title: Recovery Audits for Downstream Tariff Refunds
one_liner: A contingency-fee recovery-audit firm that mines buyers' AP invoice history for IEEPA-era price step-ups and files contract claims against suppliers who pocketed the tariff refund.
customer: Mid-market companies that paid tariff-inflated prices but were not importer of record: hospital systems and GPOs, restaurant groups, distributors, contractors, regional retailers. They pay 20-30% of dollars recovered. Secondary buyers: importers who want a defensible refund-sharing allocation, and plaintiffs' firms that need per-customer surcharge damages.
problem: Importers stand to receive roughly $166B of IEEPA refunds. Downstream buyers who paid blended, un-itemized price increases have no easy way to size or claim their share. A commercial litigator quoted by CFO.com says his team reads hundreds of thousands of invoices by hand to compare pre-tariff and tariff-period pricing, and that many suppliers keep the refund unless asked. In parallel, at least 25 customer suits (Amazon, Costco, Walmart, Sony and others) plead unjust enrichment. Plaintiffs will need per-customer surcharge data that nobody has assembled.
solution: Ingest a buyer's AP/ERP invoice line-item export (or PDFs via extraction). Normalize SKUs and suppliers. Detect step-changes in unit price against control SKUs and commodity indices around the tariff effective dates. Infer country of origin and HTS duty exposure from public tariff tables. Estimate the IEEPA-attributable overcharge per supplier. Then generate claim packets keyed to each contract's price-adjustment, cost-pass-through or MFN clauses, with demand-letter templates and a supplier-response tracker. Start with contracts that have explicit surcharge or cost-plus language, where recovery is strongest. Partner with one or two commercial litigation boutiques for enforcement, and have human analysts review the top claims. Second product: a refund-allocation ledger for importers and distributors that want to share refunds with customers, as Williams-Sonoma and O'Reilly are doing. Third product: a damages engine for class counsel.
why_now: The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs in February 2026. CBP's CAPE refund portal opened April 20, 2026. CBP had paid $100B by August 7, and CAPE Phase 3 for finally liquidated entries starts October 6, 2026. An Atlanta Fed survey (September 24) says most companies will hold refunds as cash. A trade court also ruled the 10% global tariff illegal on May 7, so more refund waves may follow. Contract-notice and limitation windows are running now.
revenue_model: 20-30% contingency on recovered dollars. Flat $15-50k fee for importer-side allocation reports. Per-matter fees from plaintiffs' firms. Possible later add-on: an expected-value model for funds that buy refund claims.
non_obvious_insight: For downstream buyers the refund is not a customs-law problem. It is an AP-data forensics problem, the same shape as classic recovery audits (freight, telecom, sales tax), which are paid on contingency, and the recovery-audit firms have not pivoted to it. The evidence shows the gap is manual labor: CFO.com describes lawyers examining 'hundreds of thousands of invoices' to find blended tariff pricing (https://www.cfo.com/news/these-businesses-didnt-pay-tariffs-theyre-seeking-refunds-anyway-Glen-Frost-Tim-Meyer/823107/). At least 25 customer suits need per-customer surcharge data (https://www.cfodive.com/news/amazon-companies-fighting-centralized-tariff-refund-suits-costco-cfo/830814/). Refund claims are also being sold at steep discounts (American Eagle sold $68.9M of claims for $18.6M), which shows the claims are being priced without data (https://www.supplychaindive.com/news/retailers-eager-for-cash-sell-off-rights-to-potential-tariff-refunds/827064/). CBP paid $100B by August 7 (https://www.supplychaindive.com/news/cbp-has-paid-100b-in-ieepa-tariff-refunds/827257/). Main risk: B2B pass-through litigation is largely untested, so lead with contract-backed claims.
first_30_days: Pick 3 verticals with blended pricing and heavy AP volume (medical/dental supply buyers, restaurant groups, HVAC/plumbing contractors, regional grocers). Offer a free 'tariff exposure scan' from 12 months of AP export and run it on 3-5 pilot datasets. Sign a contingency engagement with a trade or commercial litigation boutique for enforcement. Build supplier claim-packet templates for the 10 most common contract clause types. Aim for the first demand letters in week 4 and first recovered dollars inside 90 days.

title: Fire-Season Vaults for Fandom Collectors
angle: Pairing 1: Climate adaptation x Gaming/entertainment/live experiences/fandoms
one_liner: Red-Flag-Warning-triggered pickup and insured off-site storage for graded cards, comics, sealed games and memorabilia kept in wildfire-zone homes.
customer: Collectors holding $50K-$2M of graded trading cards, comics, sealed games and signed memorabilia in wildfire-zone ZIPs or on last-resort plans such as the California FAIR Plan (696,562 policies in June 2026).
problem: A closet of graded cards can be worth more than the contents limit on a distressed-market homeowners policy. Collectibles are usually capped or need scheduling, which retreating carriers avoid. Evacuations give minutes. Vaults exist, but storage is a one-time decision with no urgency trigger, and nobody sells 'fire season' as a product.
solution: Three steps. (1) Photograph and catalog the collection with a card-scanning app and a live price feed, producing a claim-ready inventory. (2) From June to November, the top slice of value moves to a bonded vault under agreed-value cover from a specialty coverholder. (3) The remainder goes in a pre-tagged go-case, and on a Red Flag Warning or evacuation warning within N miles a bonded courier collects it within 4 hours, or the owner drops it at a partner card shop. Everything is returned in December.
why_now: The trading-card boom (Pokemon at 85B+ cards, a $28M Kickstarter TCG, blind-box resale above RMB 1,000 with VCs funding the resale layer) has turned closets into six-figure assets. FAIR Plan exposure hit $768B (secondary source) with a 29.1% rate hike. New carriers expanding under California's Sustainable Insurance Strategy have said nothing about scheduled personal property.
revenue_model: Annual fee of about 0.6-1.2% of stored declared value (storage plus insurance), a $150-400 courier trigger fee per activation, and commission on the agreed-value policy. An average $250K customer is worth about $2.5K a year.
non_obvious_insight: Insurers are retreating from the house, not from the objects. Fandom wealth is small, portable and already authenticated (slab cert numbers), so it is the one wildfire-zone asset you can move in a single trip and value without an adjuster. The business is logistics plus underwriting data, not a vault.
first_30_days: Pre-sell 30 founding memberships through Discord, Reddit and 10 card and comic shops in fire-prone ZIPs (Altadena, Topanga, Santa Rosa, Boulder foothills). Partner with an existing vault and a Lloyd's coverholder rather than building either. Run the first live drill when Santa Ana wind season starts in October-November.

title: Turnkey Six-Bed Care Homes for Nurse-Operators
one_liner: A licensing-and-operations platform that turns ordinary houses into small licensed residential care homes run by nurses and experienced aides.
customer: Nurses, CNAs and senior aides (including immigrant health workers) who want to own and run a home, plus small investors and families who own a suitable house.
problem: Insiders think the senior-housing gap ($275B, about 549k units by 2028) needs towers, REIT capital and 3-5 year development. Yet many states license 4-10 bed homes in normal single-family zoning. The barriers are licensing know-how, fire and ADA retrofits, staffing plans and a steady flow of admissions, not capital.
solution: A 90-day licensing sprint: zoning and state licensing packet, retrofit checklist, insurance, policies and procedures. Then staffing playbooks (1:3 to 1:6 ratios), charting, medication and compliance software, an admissions pipeline from hospital discharge planners who can't find beds, and financing partners (HELOC, sale-leaseback, small-investor pools). Start with states that have small-home license categories (for example Washington adult family homes, Arizona assisted-living homes and California small RCFEs).
why_now: Occupancy is at 90.1%, the highest since 2007. Inventory growth was 0.4% in Q1 2026, the lowest on record, and nothing new arrives before 2030. Hospital discharge teams are desperate for beds, and seniors hold a record $14.92T in home equity.
revenue_model: $6-12k onboarding fee per home, 5-8% management or software fee on revenue, and a placement fee from families where permitted. Later a captive group-purchasing and insurance program.
non_obvious_insight: Supply can appear in 6 months if the constraint is permission and playbooks, not concrete. One nurse-operator with a 5-bedroom house at $5-7k per resident per month can rival a mid-size facility's per-bed economics with no construction.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 prospective operators through nursing-school and CNA Facebook groups. Sell a $2,500 feasibility-and-licensing sprint, publish a 'how to license a six-bed home in [state]' guide as lead-gen, and line up one hospital discharge planner as a first referral source.

title: Secret-Shopper Audits of Government Algorithms
one_liner: Submit synthetic applicants and questions to public benefits systems, chatbots and eligibility tools to measure real error and denial rates, then sell the evidence.
customer: State auditors and legislative oversight offices, legal-aid funders, civil-rights litigators, and government AI vendors that want an independent seal before a contract renewal.
problem: State and local buyers cannot audit the AI they bought, and no one owns post-award monitoring. Michigan's fraud detector wrongly accused 40,000 people and cost $20M plus $78M for a replacement. Contracts run 7 years with only 3% of provisions covering cybersecurity.
solution: Run agent-driven synthetic-case testers against public-facing eligibility screeners, 311 and permit chatbots, and (with authorization) internal decision tools. Publish error-rate and disparity reports with reproducible test cases. Offer a continuous monitoring subscription to buyers.
why_now: Cities and counties have moved from pilots to production AI, and the Glass/Sourcewell marketplace pilot covers about 120 agencies. Agentic testers are cheap in 2026, and Michigan makes the harm undeniable.
revenue_model: $30-120K per audit engagement, $5-15K per month for monitoring, and grant-funded public-interest audits. Vendors pay for certified re-tests.
non_obvious_insight: Public-interest audit funders and state auditors already have budgets and mandate but no measurement tool. The synthetic-case method needs no vendor cooperation and no data access.
first_30_days: Run a free audit of 10 public-facing city or state chatbots and publish the findings. Send the report to state auditors and legal-aid funders. Sign one paid audit from a funder or auditor.

title: Capacity-Attested Wishes Recordings for Estate Attorneys
angle: Pairing 1: Aging & silver economy x Creator economy / AI provenance
one_liner: Elder-law attorneys add a clinician-scored capacity note and a hash-sealed, attorney-controlled recording of the client's stated wishes to every will or trust signing, so heirs cannot wave the evidence away as a deepfake or as undue influence.
customer: Solo and small-firm elder-law and estate attorneys (they pay per client and mark it up), plus trust companies and bank wealth desks that handle contested-estate risk.
problem: A roughly $6T wealth transfer is under way, probate and estate cases rose about 32% from 2020 to 2024, and the heirs are Gen X and millennial executors. Cheap voice and video cloning means any real recording of 'what Dad said' can now be dismissed as fake, and undue-influence contests keep coming. Many attorneys avoid video because a shaky performance can backfire. Solo agers with no family have nobody to vouch for their wishes at all.
solution: A packaged signing workflow. (1) A 20-minute structured capacity assessment by a telehealth geriatric nurse practitioner or neuropsychologist, timed to the signing day. (2) A guided recording captured in an app that signs at capture with device attestation and a C2PA-style manifest, plus an independent RFC 3161 timestamp. The attorney decides what is retained. (3) An escrow vault that releases to the named executor on receipt of a death certificate. Output is a one-page verification link a probate judge can check without trusting the platform.
why_now: The oldest boomers turned 80 in 2026. FDA-cleared Alzheimer's blood tests (May and Oct 2025) will create a large biomarker-positive but still-competent population whose later wills will be attacked. C2PA 2.3 is mature and TikTok joined in Jul 2026. Voice cloning is good enough that courts and opposing counsel will start treating unsigned recordings as suspect.
revenue_model: $295-495 per client package billed to the law firm (clinician gets about $120, the rest is platform revenue), $99 a month per firm for vault storage and verification links, and later an enterprise tier for trust companies. Long-term escrow storage fees are recurring.
non_obvious_insight: The valuable evidence is not the video. It is a contemporaneous capacity finding made during the pre-dementia 'lucid window' that blood-test diagnosis is about to make very common. Provenance tech simply makes that finding, and the wishes on record, impossible to dismiss as synthetic. Attorneys buy this as malpractice and litigation insurance, not as a media product.
first_30_days: Sign 3 to 5 elder-law firms as design partners through state bar elder-law sections. Contract two geriatric NPs at a per-assessment fee. Build the capture app on off-the-shelf C2PA and timestamping libraries. Run 10 live signings at a discounted $195 and turn each into a case study for the next firm.

title: Camera-Free Certified: No-Record Spaces for Smart Glasses
one_liner: A certification, signage, staff-training and radio-detection service that lets gyms, spas, clinics and bars credibly promise 'no recording devices here' as camera glasses go mainstream.
customer: Owners of boutique gyms and pilates studios (especially women-focused), salons and spas, therapist and medical practices, schools, coworking spaces and event organizers. Their insurers are the eventual channel.
problem: Camera glasses look like ordinary eyewear. Researchers and journalists have documented men covertly filming women in gyms, workplaces and beaches. New York State courts banned them from all 1,240 courthouses in July 2026, and the Air Force, DEF CON 34 and UK Comic Con have banned them too. Yet as of July 2026 no major US gym chain had a formal smart-glasses policy, and staff have no acceptable way to check.
solution: Three tiers. (1) A policy kit with signage, member-agreement language and staff scripts ($29-49/month). (2) A 'Camera-Free Certified' badge with mystery audits, listed in a consumer directory of no-record places. (3) A discreet front-desk appliance or app that passively scans for the Bluetooth and Wi-Fi signals glasses emit and quietly alerts staff. Start with the kit and badge, and add detection once there are customers.
why_now: Smart-glasses sales climbed after Meta's Ray-Ban Display launch in late 2025. In 2026 scandals reached the mainstream, Meta bricked units with tampered recording LEDs, and institutions began banning them in a burst. Venue owners now face the liability question first.
revenue_model: $39-299 per month per venue by tier, plus one-time detection hardware, audit fees, and later insurer referral fees for certified venues.
non_obvious_insight: Bans fail without enforcement, and enforcement fails without a socially acceptable way to check. The moat is the certification norm, like 'smoke-free' or 'kosher', not the detector, which is a commodity. Women-only gyms and studios are the beachhead because 'safe to change here' is a direct marketing hook, and once one studio in a town is certified its competitors have to follow.
first_30_days: Ship the policy kit and printable signage in week one. Pitch 30 boutique studios, spas and therapist offices with a 'be the first certified venue in your city' offer. Aim for 10 paying at about $39/month. Build a Raspberry Pi or phone-based BLE scanning prototype with one pilot studio and launch a simple map of certified spaces.

title: Seller-Financing Rails for Paid-Off Homeowners
one_liner: A compliant seller-carry-in-a-box that lets free-and-clear homeowners become the bank, with underwriting, servicing, tax packaging and a note-sale exit.
customer: Retiring owners with paid-off homes and large embedded gains (SF, Chicago and other coastal markets), their listing agents and attorneys, and buyers who cannot or will not take a 7.5% bank loan (self-employed, thin-file, relocating).
problem: 30-year rates are about 7.4-7.6%, 58% more sellers than buyers and 42.5% of listings have price cuts, so deals die on financing. About 40% of owner-occupied homes carry no mortgage, and their owners could earn a better yield than deposits while deferring capital-gains tax through an installment sale. Today seller-carry is a handshake plus a lawyer, with no underwriting, servicing or exit, and federal and state rules on ability-to-repay and balloons make DIY risky.
solution: A packaged workflow: buyer ability-to-repay underwriting, state-specific note and deed-of-trust documents, a licensed sub-servicer with tax and insurance escrow, installment-sale tax packets, and a standing bid to buy the note when the seller wants liquidity. Agents get a listing-side toggle, 'seller-carry available', that widens the buyer pool.
why_now: Record buyer's market with rising rates makes sellers' cheapest concession their own balance sheet. Futures now price a 5% Fed funds rate by end-2027, which makes note yields attractive, and AI document and underwriting tooling makes small-loan servicing economical.
revenue_model: 1-1.5% origination fee paid by the buyer, $25-35 per month servicing, a 1-2 point spread on note sales, and an agent subscription tier.
non_obvious_insight: The best 'rate buydown' is not paying points to a bank but becoming the bank. Free-and-clear boomers hold the largest un-deployed lending balance sheet in housing and are one compliance product away from using it. Sellers with gains above the primary-residence exclusion also get a tax reason to spread proceeds over years.
first_30_days: Choose one state with a workable seller-finance framework and partner with a licensed originator and servicer there. Recruit 30 listing agents from local groups. Sell a $499 flat seller-carry consult to 10 sellers and track how many close. Have counsel sign off on the federal seller-financing exemption conditions before any live deal.
